venues.d: Mughal splendour on 32 acres — for one year, judged the finest hotel on earth, and it shows.
The Maharaja's own former residence — 47 acres of gardens and the definitive Jaipur address.
A 1729 royal residence reborn as a jewel-box of fantastical wallpapers — the most personal palace in the city.
A 230-year-old warrior fort on a granite hill, reborn as a dramatic all-suite retreat.
A 225-year-old family haveli inside the old walls — frescoed, romantic, and quietly grand.
A palatial modern fort of a resort on the road to Amber — grand-scale Rajput theatre.
Royal Indian dining on gold-plated tableware beneath Florentine ceilings — the grandest table in Jaipur.
Considered Rajasthani and international cooking in the most decorated hotel in the city — faultless, and framed by fort-walled gardens.
Cobalt-blue Italian fantasy under tented canopies and mango trees — the chicest room in Jaipur.

venues.n: Amber Fort (Amer Fort) & the Sheesh Mahal
venues.d: The Kachhwaha capital before Jaipur existed: honey-coloured sandstone and marble rising off a hillside, with the Sheesh Mahal's mirror-work catching a single flame into a thousand. Come at 8am before the crowds, and ask your hotel to arrange a private guided walk of the Diwan-e-Khas and Sukh Niwas before the guides start herding.

venues.n: The ascent to Amber — jeep, not elephant
venues.d: The postcard is the caparisoned elephant climbing to the Suraj Pol, but the welfare questions are real and increasingly hard to ignore. The dignified choice for a multi-gen group is the open 4WD jeep up the ramp, or better still a morning at a walk-alongside sanctuary like Elefantastic near the fort where children meet the elephants on their own terms.

Still the working home of the Jaipur royal family, which is exactly why the private Chandra Mahal tour matters: you climb through the seven-storey palace the public never sees, ending on the peacock-painted upper floors with a butler and a view over the whole pink grid. The Baradari courtyard is where you take tea between the Pritam Niwas Chowk's four seasonal gates.

The 953-window honeycomb screen the royal women watched the street from, unseen. Everyone photographs the facade from the coffee shop across Badi Chaupar; far fewer go inside and up to the top-floor jharokhas for the light through pink lattice. Best in the first hour of morning sun.

Sawai Jai Singh II's obsession made stone: nineteen giant astronomical instruments, including the world's largest sundial, that still tell the time to the second. It reads as sculpture to the eye and as pure science to the mind — a rare thing to hand a curious teenager. Take the licensed guide; the instruments are meaningless without one.

The muscular military fort above Amber, connected by subterranean passage, and home of Jaivana — one of the largest wheeled cannons ever cast, and never fired in anger. Less about palaces, more about engineering: water-harvesting tanks, ramparts, the old foundry. A good counterpoint for the men and boys after a morning of mirror-work.

The palace that appears to float on Man Sagar Lake, four of its five storeys submerged. You don't go in — you stop on the lakeshore at dusk when the light softens and migratory birds settle, a five-minute pause on the way to or from Amber that is pure Rajput romance.

Rajasthan's oldest museum, a fantastical Indo-Saracenic pile by Samuel Swinton Jacob, floodlit gold after dark. Inside: Mughal miniatures, an Egyptian mummy, and the famous carpet collection. Worth the visit for the building alone, and the lit-up evening view from Ram Niwas Garden is a set piece.

A jeweller's private obsession made public: some 4,000 pieces of Indian tribal and antique silver, gold and adornment across two floors, curated with a connoisseur's eye. For anyone shopping the trousseau or simply in love with Indian craft, it recalibrates what 'good' looks like before you buy a thing.

The historic gem and jewellery bazaar, and the front door to Jaipur's kundan, meenakari and polki trade. The real business happens in the family workshops in the lanes behind, where a discreet introduction — best arranged through your hotel or advisor — gets you sitting down with a house that has cut stones for generations, not a shopfront.

Jaipur's most storied jewellery house, jewellers to maharajas and, over the years, to a long list of international collectors. Go for the private viewing upstairs rather than the counter: enamelled Mughal-revival pieces and old-cut diamonds brought out one tray at a time over tea. The benchmark against which the rest of the city is judged.

The textile heart of the walled city: bolts of Bandhani and Leheriya tie-dye, Sanganeri block-print by the metre, mojari and jutti leatherwork. This is where you kit out the home and the trousseau in colour — send a member of staff or your advisor ahead to hold aside the good pieces so the family isn't bargaining in the heat.

Below the triple-arched Tripolia gate, the lane of lac-bangle makers where you watch artisans work molten lac over a flame and set it with mirror and stone. A small, tactile, wonderfully un-touristy stop for a bride's chooda or simply to see a living craft that hasn't moved buildings in generations.

venues.n: Blue pottery ateliers (Kripal Kumbh & the Sanganeri Gate lanes)
venues.d: Jaipur's signature cobalt-and-white glazed ware, a Persian craft the city made its own — no potter's clay in it at all, but quartz. Kripal Singh Shekhawat's studio kept the art alive; a visit to a working atelier lets you commission tiles or a dinner service for the house rather than buy off a shelf.

venues.n: Sanganer — the fine block-print & handmade paper town
venues.d: Bagru's more delicate cousin: fine Sanganeri florals on white grounds, plus the handmade-paper mills that supply the world. Closer to the city than Bagru and easily paired with a workshop visit, it's the source many of the boutique labels quietly buy from.

A restored 16th-century pink-sandstone haveli near Amber, turned into a jewel of a museum devoted to hand block-printing — living demonstrations of carving and printing, and a shop that sets the standard. A civilised, air-cooled counterpoint to the fort, and it won a UNESCO cultural-conservation award for the restoration.

The perfectly symmetrical criss-cross stairway stepwell a short walk from Amber Fort — a 16th-century community tank that is pure geometry, and blessedly cool. Go early, before the influencer crowd; it pairs naturally with a morning at the fort and the Anokhi haveli.

A temple complex tucked into a pink-rock gorge, with seven sacred water tanks fed by a natural spring and, yes, a resident troop of macaques. Come at golden hour for the ridge-top Sun Temple view over the city — atmospheric, a little wild, and genuinely off most first-time itineraries.

The most photographed modern gateway in the city: a run of arches painted end to end with Rajasthan's regions and motifs, opening onto Asia's largest circular garden. Not old, but a genuine crowd-pleaser and a guaranteed portrait for the family album — go at first light to have the colonnade to yourselves.

The tiered Mughal-style pleasure garden a maharaja built for his queen, with painted pavilions, fountains and terraces climbing the hillside. A calm, green half-hour away from the walled-city crush, lovely in the soft light of late afternoon and rarely crowded.

A restored Krishna garden-and-temple at the foot of the Nahargarh hills on the road to Amber — carved marble columns, lattices and terraces, the sort of serene, film-set setting locals use for celebrations. An easy, pretty pause to fold into the Amber run.

Charles Correa's masterwork of an arts centre, its nine-square plan a modern echo of Jaipur's own mandala city grid. Galleries, theatres and a good café inside a building that architects fly in to see — the cultured, contemporary side of a city usually pitched as pure heritage.

A serene modern temple in white Makrana marble below the Moti Dungri fort, glowing when floodlit after dark. Quiet, cool and beautifully carved — a peaceful, veg-and-Jain-friendly stop that families of every generation take to.

Jaipur's most beloved Ganesh shrine, below a private Scottish-castle-style palace on the hill, thronged with the faithful especially on Wednesdays. A short, meaningful darshan for those who want the living-faith Jaipur, not just the museum one.

The Krishna temple at the heart of the City Palace gardens, its deity brought from Vrindavan by the city's founder, where thousands gather for the aartis through the day. Time your City Palace visit around one of the seven daily darshans for something the guidebook photos can't convey.

venues.n: 1135 AD at Amber Fort — royal dining
venues.d: Dinner inside the fort itself, in candlelit halls hung with gilt and glass, on recipes once guarded by the palace kitchens. Book the private Sheesh Mahal room and let them build a Rajasthani thali; it turns a sightseeing day into an occasion, and the vegetarian menu is deep and effortless.

The old Rambagh banqueting hall — frescoed, chandeliered, palatial — serving the royal cuisines of Rajasthan, Awadh, Punjab and Hyderabad off gold-rimmed plates. Even if you're not staying at the Taj's flagship palace hotel, dinner here (and a Polo Bar nightcap) is the grandest table in the city.

venues.n: High tea at SUJÁN Rajmahal Palace
venues.d: The former royal guest palace, reborn in bold heritage-print interiors, where afternoon tea is served on the lawns among portraits of the family who hosted Jackie Kennedy and the Queen here. A witty, intimate, only-in-Jaipur way to spend a slow afternoon between forts.

venues.n: Pink City heritage walk at dawn
venues.d: The old city wakes slowly — flower sellers, temple bells, the wholesale markets before the shutters go up — and a private guided walk through the chowkris and hidden havelis at first light is the single best way to read Jai Singh's planned grid. Cool, quiet, and endlessly photogenic.

Hands in the masala: a home or poolside masterclass in dal-baati-churma, gatte ki sabzi and the sweets, almost entirely vegetarian and Jain-adaptable by default. The palace hotels (SUJÁN Rajmahal, Rambagh) run polished versions; a home kitchen with a local cook is the warmer, more personal one for a family.

Jaipur is the spiritual home of Indian polo, and the winter season still draws the old sporting set to the grounds by Rambagh. Catch a match if the calendar aligns, or simply take a drink at the Polo Bar among the trophies and the famous walnut travelling bar — the city's most patrician afternoon.

The slender 1749 victory tower rising over Tripolia Bazaar, its spiral stair climbing to one of the few open rooftop views inside the walled city. A quiet, quirky ten-minute detour that puts the whole pink grid at your feet, and almost nobody bothers.

Jaipur's green lung, ringed by a walking track, an enormous tricolour and rose gardens, with the white-marble statue of the astronomer-king Jai Singh II at its edge. A civilised early-morning walk for a family staying in the leafy C-Scheme quarter, before the heat.

The 'pride of Asia' — a meringue-pink Art Moderne movie palace where the interiors are the real show and the audience cheers the star's first frame. Book the box seats for a Bollywood matinee; it's kitsch, joyous and utterly Jaipur, and children never forget it.

venues.n: Jaipur Modern & the design boutiques of C-Scheme
venues.d: The city's contemporary-design side: concept stores and ateliers like Jaipur Modern, Hot Pink and the Anokhi flagship, where Rajasthani craft is cut for a modern home and wardrobe. The considered, air-conditioned alternative to bazaar bargaining for those furnishing a house.

venues.n: Studio visit to a miniature painter
venues.d: Jaipur keeps the Rajput-Mughal miniature tradition alive — squirrel-hair brushes, stone pigments, gold leaf, a peacock painted on a grain of rice. A private studio sitting, arranged through your advisor, lets you commission a family piece and watch a craft measured in years of apprenticeship.

venues.n: Sunset drinks at a rooftop over the walled city
venues.d: As the light drops, the pink grid glows and the rooftops fill — spots above Hawa Mahal and along the old city put the Palace of Winds and the Nahargarh ridge in one frame. A gentle, unstructured hour to close a day of forts, chai or something stronger in hand.

venues.n: Bespoke perfume & attar at Sugandh Co / the ittar makers
venues.d: Jaipur's old attar tradition — natural oil-based ittars of rose, khus, oudh and the monsoon-earth 'mitti' — blended to order in tiny walled-city shops. A small, sensory, deeply personal thing to carry home, and a lovely gift to layer into the trousseau.
Rare whiskies and colonial-era charm amid polo memorabilia — the grandest nightcap in Jaipur.
A cobalt-blue Italian dream under garden canopies — as much a scene as a drink.
